name: Market Knowledge Coordination
description: Descriptive expectation that decentralized prices and exchange can aggregate dispersed information and coordinate resources.
boundaryStatement: An empirical mechanism claim, not a claim that every market outcome is just.

poles.negative: Market prices generally fail to coordinate dispersed information and resources
poles.positive: Decentralized prices and exchange can often coordinate dispersed information and resources

name: Market Power and Concentration
description: Descriptive expectation that market institutions can generate durable private concentration, monopoly, or dependency.
boundaryStatement: Does not by itself imply a particular antitrust, ownership, or regulatory remedy.

poles.negative: Competitive pressures usually prevent durable private concentration or dependency
poles.positive: Market institutions can generate durable concentration, monopoly, or dependency

name: State Administrative Capacity
description: Descriptive expectation that state institutions can competently implement complex policy programs under suitable conditions.
boundaryStatement: Separate from whether those programs are legitimate or desirable.

poles.negative: State institutions generally cannot competently execute complex policy programs
poles.positive: State institutions can competently execute complex policy programs under suitable conditions

name: Political Incentives and Capture
description: Descriptive expectation that public institutions are vulnerable to organized interests, rent seeking, and insider incentives.
boundaryStatement: Does not entail that private institutions are free from analogous power problems.

poles.negative: Public institutions usually overcome organized-interest and insider incentives
poles.positive: Public institutions are often vulnerable to organized interests, rent seeking, and insider incentives

name: Democratic Decision Capacity
description: Descriptive confidence that democratic procedures can aggregate information and preferences, correct errors, and reach workable collective decisions.
boundaryStatement: Distinct from the normative legitimacy of democracy.

poles.negative: Democratic procedures are generally poor at aggregating information and correcting collective errors
poles.positive: Democratic procedures can often aggregate information and correct collective errors

name: Expert Knowledge Capacity
description: Descriptive expectation that specialized expertise can improve collective decisions under appropriate accountability structures.
boundaryStatement: Does not by itself justify technocratic insulation from accountability.

poles.negative: Delegation to specialized expertise rarely improves collective decisions
poles.positive: Specialized expertise can substantially improve collective decisions under appropriate institutions

name: Cultural Malleability
description: Descriptive expectation that norms, identities, and cultural practices respond substantially to institutions, incentives, and policy.
boundaryStatement: Distinct from the normative desirability of cultural change.

poles.negative: Cultural patterns are strongly persistent and resist deliberate institutional change
poles.positive: Cultural patterns can change substantially in response to institutions, incentives, and policy

name: Decentralized Coordination Capacity
description: Descriptive expectation that voluntary, local, polycentric, or federated institutions can solve coordination problems without a single central director.
boundaryStatement: Does not imply every public good can be privately supplied.

poles.negative: Coordination problems generally require a single central director
poles.positive: Voluntary, local, polycentric, or federated institutions can often solve coordination problems without one central director

name: Class and Exploitation
description: Descriptive claim that class relations and control of productive assets systematically generate exploitation or asymmetric workplace power.
boundaryStatement: A mechanism claim that should not be inferred merely from support for redistribution.

poles.negative: Class ownership relations do not systematically generate exploitation or asymmetric workplace power
poles.positive: Class ownership relations systematically generate exploitation or asymmetric workplace power

name: Capital Accumulation and Crisis
description: Descriptive claim that capitalist accumulation tends toward concentration, instability, or recurrent crisis mechanisms.
boundaryStatement: Distinct from ordinary claims that individual markets sometimes fail.

poles.negative: Capitalist accumulation has no systematic tendency toward concentration or recurrent crisis
poles.positive: Capitalist accumulation tends toward concentration, instability, or recurrent crisis mechanisms

name: Ideology and Hegemony
description: Descriptive claim that beliefs, culture, and institutions systematically reproduce or legitimate structures of power.
boundaryStatement: Does not imply that every belief is reducible to class interest or propaganda.

poles.negative: Beliefs and cultural institutions are largely independent of structural power
poles.positive: Beliefs and cultural institutions can systematically reproduce or legitimate structures of power

name: Nation Formation
description: Descriptive claim that national identities are socially and institutionally produced and historically reproduced rather than simply given.
boundaryStatement: Distinct from whether nations deserve self-determination.

poles.negative: National identities are largely fixed or given independently of institutions and historical construction
poles.positive: National identities are substantially produced and reproduced through institutions and historical processes

name: Patriarchy and Social Reproduction
description: Descriptive claim that gendered power and social reproduction systematically structure institutions, work, family, and opportunities.
boundaryStatement: A structural explanatory claim, not a generic endorsement of sex equality.

poles.negative: Gendered power and social reproduction do not systematically structure major institutions and opportunities
poles.positive: Gendered power and social reproduction systematically structure institutions and opportunities

name: Imperialism and Dependency
description: Descriptive claim that international political-economic relations can reproduce domination or dependency across states and peoples.
boundaryStatement: Distinct from the normative view that any particular intervention is wrong.

poles.negative: International political-economic relations do not systematically reproduce dependency or external domination
poles.positive: International political-economic relations can systematically reproduce dependency or external domination

name: Ecological Limits to Growth
description: Descriptive expectation that biophysical constraints can limit or materially alter the feasibility of indefinite growth in throughput.
boundaryStatement: Does not settle whether GDP, welfare, or technological progress must decline.

poles.negative: Biophysical constraints place no important long-run limits on material throughput because substitution and innovation can overcome them
poles.positive: Biophysical constraints can materially limit the feasibility of indefinite growth in material throughput

name: Collective Action Capacity
description: Descriptive claim that groups can overcome free-rider and coordination problems under identifiable institutional conditions.
boundaryStatement: Not a claim that collective action is always efficient or benign.

poles.negative: Free-rider problems generally prevent groups from sustaining collective solutions
poles.positive: Groups can overcome free-rider and coordination problems under identifiable institutional conditions

name: Institutional Path Dependence
description: Descriptive claim that inherited institutions constrain later feasible choices and reform trajectories.
boundaryStatement: Does not imply that institutional change is impossible or undesirable.

poles.negative: Inherited institutional arrangements place little constraint on feasible later reforms
poles.positive: Inherited institutions substantially constrain later feasible choices and reform trajectories

name: Structural Historical Change
description: Descriptive claim that large-scale political change is substantially shaped by structural social and economic forces rather than only individual preferences or leaders.
boundaryStatement: Allows agency and contingency while measuring the claimed explanatory importance of structure.

poles.negative: Large-scale political change is mainly explained by individual leaders and choices rather than structural forces
poles.positive: Large-scale political change is substantially shaped by structural social and economic forces
